**1. Observation schedule – how to spread the 40 monthly audits across the three shifts** | Shift | Typical nurse count (example) | % of unit staff | # of observations per month* | |-------|------------------------------|-----------------|-----------------------------| | Day | 12 | 37 % | 15 | | Evening | 10 | 31 % | 13 | | Night | 10 | 31 % | 12 | \*If the actual nurse‑to‑shift distribution differs, simply replace the numbers in the “Typical nurse count” column and recalculate: ``` Observations for a shift = 40 × (nurses on that shift ÷ total nurses) ``` Round to the nearest whole number so the totals add to 40. If you prefer an equal‑split schedule (e.g., when staffing is roughly even), assign **14** observations to Day, **13** to Evening and **13** to Night. **Scheduling mechanics** 1. **Create a monthly calendar grid** – one row per shift, columns for the 15–20 observation slots that month. 2. **Random‑select nurses** – use a simple random number generator or a pre‑made list of all nurses on each shift; pick the required number of unique nurse identifiers per slot. 3. **Assign auditors** – alternate auditors so that each auditor covers every shift over the course of the month (e.g., Auditor A: Day, Night; Auditor B: Evening, Day). 4. **Record observation windows** – note the exact time window (e.g., 08:00‑10:00) to ensure coverage across all five WHO moments. 5. **Track overlap** – schedule a few “double‑audit” slots (both auditors observe the same nurse in the same shift) once per month to gauge inter‑rater reliability. --- **2. What each auditor must record for an observation to be considered valid** | Field | Required content | Why it matters | |-------|------------------|----------------| | **Date & time stamp** | Exact date and hour of the hand‑hygiene event | Enables trend analysis and audit timing | | **Shift** | Day / Evening / Night | Allows shift‑specific compliance rates | | **Nurse identifier** (e.g., badge number or unit code) | Unique ID, not name | Protects privacy while linking to staffing data | | **Patient/Unit** | Bed number or patient ID (de‑identified) | Contextualizes the hand‑hygiene moment | | **WHO Moment** | 1–5 (e.g., “Before touching a patient”) | Determines which step is being evaluated | | **Compliance** | Yes / No | Core metric | | **If non‑compliant, reason** | e.g., “No alcohol rub used”, “Technique incomplete”, “Time pressure” | Drives targeted interventions | | **Contextual factors** (optional but recommended) | Availability of sinks, presence of hand‑rub dispenser, patient acuity level | Helps explain patterns | | **Auditor name & signature** | Auditor A / B and a brief signature or initials | Accountability and audit trail | | **Observation method** | Direct observation vs. video review | Clarifies data source | *Validity check:* - The auditor must observe the entire hand‑hygiene action (from start to finish). - Observation must be recorded within 5 minutes of the event to avoid recall bias. - All mandatory fields must be filled; any missing field invalidates the observation. --- **3. Presenting monthly results to the unit** | Format | Content | How to deliver | |--------|---------|----------------| | **Executive summary (1‑page)** | • Overall compliance %
• Shift‑wise compliance
• WHO moment breakdown
• Key non‑compliance drivers | Email to unit leadership; display on the unit’s notice board | | **Detailed report (2–3 pages)** | • Table of raw observations (nurses, shifts, moments)
• Inter‑rater agreement % (for double audits)
• Trend line vs. previous months | Share during the monthly unit huddle; post PDF on intranet | | **Visual dashboard** | • Bar chart: compliance by shift
• Pie chart: compliance by WHO moment
• Line graph: trend over 6 months | Projected in the meeting room; embed interactive version in the unit’s shared drive | | **Action plan** | • Targeted training topics (e.g., “Proper technique for hand‑rub”)
• Resource needs (extra dispensers, signage)
• Follow‑up audit dates | Discuss during the huddle; assign owners | **Key points to emphasize** 1. **Transparency:** Show both successes and gaps so staff know where improvement is needed. 2. **Contextualization:** Link non‑compliance reasons to actionable changes (e.g., “Time pressure” → consider workflow redesign). 3. **Engagement:** Invite nurses to comment on the dashboard; use their feedback for next month’s audit focus. By structuring the observation schedule proportionally, rigorously recording each audit, and presenting results in a clear, data‑driven format, the unit will build a sustainable hand‑hygiene culture that aligns with WHO best practices.
